claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized cognitive neuroscience.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized cognitive neuroscience, but methodological barriers limit the generalizability of findings from the lab to the real world.
evidence: This is a general statement about the impact of fMRI on the field, presented as established knowledge without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Methodological barriers limit the generalizability of fMRI findings from the lab to the real world.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized cognitive neuroscience, but methodological barriers limit the generalizability of findings from the lab to the real world.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and discussion throughout the manuscript regarding generalizability concerns.

claim: Neuroscout is an end-to-end platform for analysis of naturalistic fMRI data.
source: Here, we present Neuroscout, an end-to-end platform for analysis of naturalistic fMRI data designed to facilitate the adoption of robust and generalizable research practices.
evidence: This is a direct description of the platform presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neuroscout leverages state-of-the-art machine learning models to automatically annotate stimuli from dozens of fMRI studies.
source: Neuroscout leverages state-of-the-art machine learning models to automatically annotate stimuli from dozens of fMRI studies using naturalistic stimuli—such as movies and narratives—allowing researchers to easily test neuroscientific hypotheses across multiple ecologically-valid datasets.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the platform's feature extraction capabilities and the datasets indexed.

claim: Neuroscout builds on a robust ecosystem of open tools and standards.
source: In addition, Neuroscout builds on a robust ecosystem of open tools and standards to provide an easy-to-use analysis builder and a fully automated execution engine that reduce the burden of reproducible research.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the tools and standards used throughout the manuscript (BIDS, fMRIPrep, etc.).

claim: Neuroscout makes it possible to overcome modeling challenges commonly arising in naturalistic analysis.
source: Owing to its ease of use and a high degree of automation, Neuroscout makes it possible to overcome modeling challenges commonly arising in naturalistic analysis and to easily scale analyses within and across datasets, democratizing generalizable fMRI research.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the case studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Thousands of fMRI studies mapping cognitive functions to brain anatomy are published every year.
source: Vast amounts of resources have been invested in fMRI research, and thousands of fMRI studies mapping cognitive functions to brain anatomy are published every year.
evidence: This is presented as general knowledge about the state of the field.

claim: Methodological concerns threaten the reliability of fMRI results and their generalizability from laboratory conditions to the real world.
source: Yet, increasingly urgent methodological concerns threaten the reliability of fMRI results and their generalizability from laboratory conditions to the real world.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations throughout the introduction.

claim: A key weakness of current fMRI research concerns its generalizability.
source: A key weakness of current fMRI research concerns its generalizability—that is, whether conclusions drawn from individual studies apply beyond the participant sample and experimental conditions of the original study (Turner et al., 2018; Bossier et al., 2020; Yarkoni, 2020; Szucs and Ioannidis, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Many fMRI studies attempt to isolate cognitive constructs using highly controlled and limited sets of reductive stimuli.
source: Many studies attempt to isolate cognitive constructs using highly controlled and limited sets of reductive stimuli, such as still images depicting specific classes of objects in isolation, or pure tones.
evidence: This is presented as a description of common practice in the field.

claim: Highly controlled and reductive stimuli radically differ in complexity and cognitive demand from real-world contexts.
source: However, such stimuli radically differ in complexity and cognitive demand from real-world contexts, calling into question whether resulting inferences generalize outside the laboratory to more ecological settings (Nastase et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: Predominant statistical analysis approaches generally fail to model stimulus-related variability.
source: In addition, predominant statistical analysis approaches generally fail to model stimulus-related variability.
evidence: This is presented as a known limitation in the field, supported by subsequent citation.

claim: Many fMRI studies likely overestimate the strength of their statistical evidence and their generalizability to new but equivalent stimuli.
source: As a result, many studies–and especially those relying on small stimulus sets–likely overestimate the strength of their statistical evidence and their generalizability to new but equivalent stimuli (Westfall et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: fMRI studies are frequently underpowered due to the cost of data collection.
source: Finally, since fMRI studies are frequently underpowered due to the cost of data collection, results can fail to replicate on new participant samples (Button et al., 2013; Cremers et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Naturalistic paradigms using life-like stimuli have been advocated as a way to increase the generalizability of fMRI studies.
source: Naturalistic paradigms using life-like stimuli have been advocated as a way to increase the generalizability of fMRI studies (DuPre et al., 2020; Hamilton and Huth, 2020; Nastase et al., 2020; Sonkusare et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: Stimuli such as movies and narratives feature rich, multidimensional variation.
source: Stimuli such as movies and narratives feature rich, multidimensional variation, presenting an opportunity to test hypotheses from highly controlled experiments in more ecological settings.
evidence: This is presented as a characteristic of naturalistic stimuli.

claim: Challenges in modeling naturalistic data limit their impact despite the proliferation of openly available naturalistic datasets.
source: Yet, despite the proliferation of openly available naturalistic datasets, challenges in modeling these data limit their impact.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent discussion of modeling challenges.

claim: Naturalistic features are difficult to characterize and co-occur with potential confounds in complex and unexpected ways.
source: Naturalistic features are difficult to characterize and co-occur with potential confounds in complex and unexpected ways (Nastase et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: Annotating events at fine temporal resolution in naturalistic stimuli is laborious.
source: This is exacerbated by the laborious task of annotating events at fine temporal resolution, which limits the number of variables that can realistically be defined and modelled.
evidence: This is presented as a known challenge in naturalistic fMRI research.

claim: Isolating relationships between specific features of stimuli and brain activity in naturalistic data is especially challenging.
source: As a result, isolating relationships between specific features of the stimuli and brain activity in naturalistic data is especially challenging, which deters researchers from conducting naturalistic experiments and limiting re-use of existing public datasets.
evidence: This is presented as an inference from the previously stated challenges.

claim: Low reproducibility of analysis workflows is a fundamental concern limiting the impact of fMRI research.
source: A related and more fundamental concern limiting the impact of fMRI research is the low reproducibility of analysis workflows.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations and discussion.

claim: Incomplete reporting practices in combination with flexible and variable analysis methods are a major culprit for low reproducibility.
source: Incomplete reporting practices in combination with flexible and variable analysis methods (Carp, 2012) are a major culprit.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: A large-scale effort to test identical hypotheses in the same dataset by 70 teams found a high degree of variability in the results.
source: For instance, a recent large-scale effort to test identical hypotheses in the same dataset by 70 teams found a high degree of variability in the results, with different teams often reaching different conclusions (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Re-executing the original analysis from an existing publication is rarely possible due to insufficient provenance and reliance on exclusively verbal descriptions.
source: Even re-executing the original analysis from an existing publication is rarely possible, due to insufficient provenance and a reliance on exclusively verbal descriptions of statistical models and analytical workflows (Ghosh et al., 2017; Mackenzie-Graham et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) standard has galvanized efforts to foster reproducible practices across the data analysis lifecycle.
source: The recent proliferation of community-led tools and standards—most notably the Brain Imaging Data Structure (Gorgolewski et al., 2016) standard—has galvanized efforts to foster reproducible practices across the data analysis lifecycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the BIDS standard and subsequent discussion of its impact.

claim: A growing number of data archives now host hundreds of publicly available neuroimaging datasets, including dozens of naturalistic fMRI datasets.
source: A growing number of data archives, such as OpenNeuro (Markiewicz et al., 2021c), now host hundreds of publicly available neuroimaging datasets, including dozens of naturalistic fMRI datasets.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to OpenNeuro.

claim: Standardized quality control and preprocessing pipelines facilitate the analysis of public neuroimaging datasets.
source: The development of standardized quality control and preprocessing pipelines, such as MRIQC (Esteban et al., 2017), fmriprep (Esteban et al., 2019; Esteban et al., 2022), and C-PAC (Craddock et al., 2013), facilitate their analysis and can be launched on emerging cloud-based platforms, such as https://brainlife.io/about/ (Avesani et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific preprocessing pipelines and platforms.

claim: fMRI model specification and estimation remains challenging to standardize.
source: However, fMRI model specification and estimation remains challenging to standardize, and typically results in bespoke modeling pipelines that are not often shared, and can be difficult to re-use.
evidence: This is presented as a known limitation in the field.

claim: Assembling tools into a complete and reproducible workflow remains out of reach for many scientists due to substantial technical challenges.
source: Unfortunately, despite the availability of a rich ecosystem of tools, assembling them into a complete and reproducible workflow remains out of reach for many scientists due to substantial technical challenges.
evidence: This is presented as an observation about the current state of the field.

claim: Neuroscout improves current research practice in three key ways.
source: Neuroscout improves current research practice in three key ways.
evidence: This is a summary statement that is elaborated in the subsequent text.

claim: Neuroscout provides an easy-to-use interface for reproducible analysis of BIDS datasets.
source: First, Neuroscout provides an easy-to-use interface for reproducible analysis of BIDS datasets, seamlessly integrating a diverse ecosystem of community-developed resources into a unified workflow.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the platform's features.

claim: Neuroscout encourages re-analysis of public naturalistic datasets by providing access to hundreds of predictors extracted through state-of-the-art feature extraction algorithms.
source: Second, Neuroscout encourages re-analysis of public naturalistic datasets by providing access to hundreds of predictors extracted through an expandable set of state-of-the-art feature extraction algorithms spanning multiple stimulus modalities.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the platform's feature extraction capabilities.

claim: Neuroscout enables researchers to easily operationalize hypotheses in a uniform way across multiple datasets.
source: Finally, by using standardized model specifications and automated workflows, Neuroscout enables researchers to easily operationalize hypotheses in a uniform way across multiple (and diverse) datasets, facilitating more generalizable multi-dataset workflows such as meta-analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the case studies demonstrating multi-dataset analyses.

claim: The Neuroscout platform is composed of three primary components: a data ingestion and feature extraction server, interactive analysis creation tools, and an automated model fitting workflow.
source: The platform is composed of three primary components: a data ingestion and feature extraction server, interactive analysis creation tools, and an automated model fitting workflow.
evidence: This is a direct description of the platform architecture.

claim: All elements of the Neuroscout platform can be accessed interactively online at https://neuroscout.org.
source: All elements of the platform are seamlessly integrated and can be accessed interactively online (https://neuroscout.org).
evidence: This is a factual statement about platform accessibility.

claim: The Neuroscout server indexes a curated set of publicly available naturalistic fMRI datasets.
source: The Neuroscout server indexes a curated set of publicly available naturalistic fMRI datasets, and hosts automatically extracted annotations of visual, auditory, and linguistic events from the experimental stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of the platform's data infrastructure.

claim: Datasets in Neuroscout are harmonized, preprocessed, and ingested into a database using robust BIDS-compliant pipelines.
source: Datasets are harmonized, preprocessed, and ingested into a database using robust BIDS-compliant pipelines, facilitating future expansion.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing workflow.

claim: Annotations of stimuli are automatically extracted using pliers.
source: Annotations of stimuli are automatically extracted using pliers (McNamara et al., 2017), a comprehensive feature extraction framework supporting state-of-the-art algorithms and deep learning models (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to pliers and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Currently available features in Neuroscout include hundreds of predictors coding for low-level and mid-level properties of audiovisual stimuli, as well as natural language properties.
source: Currently available features include hundreds of predictors coding for both low-level (e.g. brightness, loudness) and mid-level (e.g. object recognition indicators) properties of audiovisual stimuli, as well as natural language properties from force aligned speech transcripts (e.g. lexical frequency annotations).
evidence: This is a description of the types of features available in the platform.

claim: The set of available predictors in Neuroscout can be easily expanded through community-driven implementation of new pliers extractors.
source: The set of available predictors can be easily expanded through community-driven implementation of new pliers extractors, as well as publicly shared repositories of deep learning models, such as HuggingFace (Wolf et al., 2020) and TensorFlowHub (Abadi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the platform's extensibility, supported by citations to model repositories.

claim: All extracted predictors are made publicly available through a well-documented application programming interface.
source: All extracted predictors are made publicly available through a well-documented application programming interface (https://neuroscout.org/api).
evidence: This is a factual statement about data accessibility.

claim: Neuroscout's interactive analysis creation tools enable easy creation of fully reproducible fMRI analyses.
source: Neuroscout's interactive analysis creation tools—available as a web application (https://neuroscout.org/builder) and python library (pyNS)—enable easy creation of fully reproducible fMRI analyses (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a description of the platform's analysis tools, with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: All elements of the multi-level statistical model in Neuroscout are formally represented using the BIDS Statistical Models specification.
source: Internally all elements of the multi-level statistical model are formally represented using the BIDS Statistical Models specification (Markiewicz et al., 2021a), ensuring transparency and reproducibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the BIDS Statistical Models specification.

claim: Finalized analyses in Neuroscout are locked from further modification and assigned a unique identifier.
source: Finalized analyses are locked from further modification, assigned a unique identifier, and packaged into a self-contained bundle.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis finalization process.

claim: Analyses in Neuroscout can be executed in a single command line using Neuroscout's automated model execution workflow.
source: Analyses can be executed in a single command line using Neuroscout's automated model execution workflow (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a description of the execution workflow, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: Neuroscout uses container technology to minimize software dependencies, facilitate installation, and ensure portability.
source: Neuroscout uses container technology (i.e. Docker and Singularity) to minimize software dependencies, facilitate installation, and ensure portability across a wide range of environments (including high performance computers (HPC) and the cloud).
evidence: This is a description of the technical implementation.

claim: Preprocessed imaging data in Neuroscout are automatically fetched using DataLad at run time.
source: At run time, preprocessed imaging data are automatically fetched using DataLad (Halchenko et al., 2021), and the analysis is executed using FitLins (Markiewicz et al., 2021b), a standardized pipeline for estimating BIDS Stats Models.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DataLad and FitLins.

claim: Thresholded statistical maps and provenance metadata from Neuroscout analyses are submitted to NeuroVault.
source: Once completed, thresholded statistical maps and provenance metadata are submitted to NeuroVault (Gorgolewski et al., 2015), a public repository for statistical maps, guaranteeing compliance to FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable) scientific principles (Wilkinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to NeuroVault and FAIR principles.

claim: Neuroscout automatically generates a bibliography that can be used in original research reports.
source: Finally, Neuroscout facilitates sharing and appropriately crediting the dataset and tools used in the analysis by automatically generating a bibliography that can be used in original research reports.
evidence: This is a description of a platform feature.

claim: Automated feature extraction and standardized model specification in Neuroscout make it easy to operationalize and test equivalent hypotheses across many datasets.
source: Automated feature extraction and standardized model specification make it easy to operationalize and test equivalent hypotheses across many datasets, spanning larger participant samples and a more diverse range of stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent demonstration of multi-dataset analyses.

claim: The validation analyses focused on three feature modalities: visual, auditory, and language.
source: We focused these analyses on three feature modalities (visual, auditory, and language), ranging from low-level features of the signal (loudness, brightness, presence of speech, and shot change), to mid-level characteristics with well established focal correlates (visual presence of buildings, faces, tools, landscape and text).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis design.

claim: For each feature and stimulus, a whole-brain univariate GLM was fit with the target feature as the sole predictor, in addition to standard nuisance covariates.
source: For each feature and stimulus, we fit a whole-brain univariate GLM with the target feature as the sole predictor, in addition to standard nuisance covariates (see Methods for details).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: Estimates across twenty studies were combined using random-effects image-based meta-analysis.
source: Finally, we combined estimates across twenty studies using random-effects image-based meta-analysis (IBMA), resulting in a consensus statistical map for each feature.
evidence: This is a description of the meta-analysis method.

claim: Robust meta-analytic activation patterns largely consistent with expectations from the existing literature were observed.
source: Even using a simple one-predictor approach, we observed robust meta-analytic activation patterns largely consistent with expectations from the existing literature (Figure 3), a strong sign of the reliability of automatically extracted predictors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 3 and comparison to literature.

claim: Activation in the primary visual cortex was observed for brightness.
source: We observed activation in the primary visual cortex for brightness (Peters et al., 2010), parahippocampal place area (PPA) activation in response to buildings and landscapes (Park and Chun, 2009; Häusler et al., 2022), visual word form area (VWFA) activation in response to text (Chen et al., 2019), and lateral occipito-temporal cortex (LOTC) and parietal activation in regions associated with action perception and action knowledge (Schone et al., 2021; Valyear et al., 2007) in response to the presence of tools on screen.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and citations to relevant literature.

claim: Parahippocampal place area (PPA) activation was observed in response to buildings and landscapes.
source: We observed activation in the primary visual cortex for brightness (Peters et al., 2010), parahippocampal place area (PPA) activation in response to buildings and landscapes (Park and Chun, 2009; Häusler et al., 2022), visual word form area (VWFA) activation in response to text (Chen et al., 2019), and lateral occipito-temporal cortex (LOTC) and parietal activation in regions associated with action perception and action knowledge (Schone et al., 2021; Valyear et al., 2007) in response to the presence of tools on screen.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and citations to relevant literature.

claim: Visual word form area (VWFA) activation was observed in response to text.
source: We observed activation in the primary visual cortex for brightness (Peters et al., 2010), parahippocampal place area (PPA) activation in response to buildings and landscapes (Park and Chun, 2009; Häusler et al., 2022), visual word form area (VWFA) activation in response to text (Chen et al., 2019), and lateral occipito-temporal cortex (LOTC) and parietal activation in regions associated with action perception and action knowledge (Schone et al., 2021; Valyear et al., 2007) in response to the presence of tools on screen.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and citations to relevant literature.

claim: Lateral occipito-temporal cortex (LOTC) and parietal activation was observed in response to the presence of tools on screen.
source: We observed activation in the primary visual cortex for brightness (Peters et al., 2010), parahippocampal place area (PPA) activation in response to buildings and landscapes (Park and Chun, 2009; Häusler et al., 2022), visual word form area (VWFA) activation in response to text (Chen et al., 2019), and lateral occipito-temporal cortex (LOTC) and parietal activation in regions associated with action perception and action knowledge (Schone et al., 2021; Valyear et al., 2007) in response to the presence of tools on screen.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and citations to relevant literature.

claim: Primary auditory cortex activation was observed in response to loudness.
source: For auditory features, we observed primary auditory cortex activation in response to loudness (Langers et al., 2007), and superior temporal sulcus and gyrus activity in response to speech (Sekiyama et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and citations to relevant literature.

claim: Superior temporal sulcus and gyrus activity was observed in response to speech.
source: For auditory features, we observed primary auditory cortex activation in response to loudness (Langers et al., 2007), and superior temporal sulcus and gyrus activity in response to speech (Sekiyama et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and citations to relevant literature.

claim: Visual shot changes yielded activations in the frontal eye fields, the precuneus, and parietal regions.
source: We also observed plausible results for visual shot changes, a feature with fewer direct analogs from the literature, which yielded activations in the frontal eye fields, the precuneus, and parietal regions areas traditionally implicated in attentional orienting and reference frame shifts (Corbetta et al., 1998; Fox et al., 2006; Kravitz et al., 2011; Rocca et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and citations to relevant literature.

claim: A failure to detect fusiform face area (FFA) activity in response to faces was observed.
source: The only notable exception was a failure to detect fusiform face area (FFA) activity in response to faces (Figure 5), an interesting result that we dissect in the following section.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Study-level results exhibited a wide range of idiosyncratic variation across datasets.
source: Crucially, although study-level results largely exhibited plausible activation patterns, a wide range of idiosyncratic variation was evident across datasets (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: For 'building', PPA activity was observed in almost every study.
source: For instance, for 'building' we observed PPA activity in almost every study.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: A divergent pattern of activity in the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) was observed across studies for 'building'.
source: However, we observed a divergent pattern of activity in the anterior temporal lobe (ATL), with some studies indicating a deactivation, others activation, and others no relationship.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The meta-analysis indicated no relationship between 'building' and the ATL, but confirmed a strong association with the PPA.
source: This dissonance was resolved in the meta-analysis, which indicated no relationship with 'building' and the ATL, but confirmed a strong association with the PPA.
evidence: This is a result from the meta-analysis.

claim: Multi-dataset meta-analytic approaches are intrinsically more robust to stimulus-specific variation than single dataset studies.
source: In contrast, multi-dataset meta-analytic approaches are intrinsically more robust to stimulus-specific variation, licensing broader generalization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed results.

claim: The absence of fusiform face area (FFA) activation for faces in naturalistic stimuli is unlikely to indicate flaws in the extant literature.
source: Given long-standing prior evidence implicating the FFA in face processing (Kanwisher et al., 1997), it is highly unlikely that these results are indicative of flaws in the extant literature.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior literature, supported by citation.

claim: The 'naive' single predictor models failed to account for complex scene dynamics present in naturalistic stimuli.
source: A more plausible explanation is that our 'naive' single predictor models failed to account for complex scene dynamics present in naturalistic stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed results.

claim: In narrative-driven movies, the presentation of faces often co-occurs with speech.
source: For example, in narrative-driven movies (the most commonly used audio-visual naturalistic stimuli) the presentation of faces often co-occurs with speech—a strong driver of brain activity.
evidence: This is presented as a known characteristic of naturalistic stimuli.

claim: Failing to account for shared variance between faces and speech can confound model estimates and mask true effects.
source: Failing to account for this shared variance can confound model estimates and mask true effects attributable to predictors of interest.
evidence: This is a general principle of statistical modeling applied to the specific context.

claim: After controlling for speech, an association between face presentation and right FFA activity was observed across 17 datasets.
source: After controlling for speech, we observed an association between face presentation and right FFA activity across 17 datasets (Figure 5; peak z=5.70).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The strength of the relationship between face presentation and right FFA remained weaker than one might expect from traditional face localizer tasks.
source: Yet, the strength of this relationship remained weaker than one might expect from traditional face localizer tasks.
evidence: This is an observation comparing the results to expectations from traditional tasks.

claim: In movies, face perception involves repeated and protracted presentation of a relatively narrow set of individual faces.
source: In movies, face perception involves repeated and protracted presentation of a relatively narrow set of individual faces.
evidence: This is presented as a characteristic of movie stimuli.

claim: There is evidence of rapid adaptation of category-selective fMRI response to individual stimuli.
source: Given evidence of rapid adaptation of category-selective fMRI response to individual stimuli (Grill-Spector et al., 1999), FFA activation in naturalistic stimuli may be attenuated by a failure to distinguish transient processes (e.g. initial encoding) from indiscriminate face exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: FFA activation in naturalistic stimuli may be attenuated by a failure to distinguish transient processes from indiscriminate face exposure.
source: Given evidence of rapid adaptation of category-selective fMRI response to individual stimuli (Grill-Spector et al., 1999), FFA activation in naturalistic stimuli may be attenuated by a failure to distinguish transient processes (e.g. initial encoding) from indiscriminate face exposure.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited evidence.

claim: Embeddings from FaceNet were used to cluster individual face presentations into groups representing distinct characters in each movie.
source: Using embeddings from FaceNet, a face recognition convolutional neural network, we clustered individual face presentations into groups representing distinct characters in each movie.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: After controlling for face adaptation, stronger effects in the right FFA were observed.
source: After controlling for face adaptation, we observed stronger effects in the right FFA (Figure 5; peak z=7.35), highlighting its sensitivity to dynamic characteristics of face presentation which cannot always be captured by traditional designs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The right FFA is sensitive to dynamic characteristics of face presentation which cannot always be captured by traditional designs.
source: After controlling for face adaptation, we observed stronger effects in the right FFA (Figure 5; peak z=7.35), highlighting its sensitivity to dynamic characteristics of face presentation which cannot always be captured by traditional designs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed results.

claim: Studies using naturalistic input are becoming increasingly common in language neuroscience.
source: Owing to their ability to provide more robust insights into real-life language processing, studies using naturalistic input (e.g. long written texts or narratives) are becoming increasingly common in language neuroscience (Andric and Small, 2015; Brennan, 2016; Nastase et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Individual studies using naturalistic stimuli are rarely representative of the many contexts in which language production and comprehension take place in daily life.
source: Yet, even when naturalistic stimuli are used, individual studies are rarely representative of the many contexts in which language production and comprehension take place in daily life (e.g. dialogues, narratives, written exchanges, etc), which raises concerns on the generalizability of their findings.
evidence: This is presented as a limitation of current research practices.

claim: Modeling covariates is particularly challenging for linguistic stimuli due to their complex hierarchical structure.
source: Additionally, modeling covariates is particularly challenging for linguistic stimuli, due to their complex hierarchical structure.
evidence: This is presented as a known challenge in linguistic research.

claim: Single studies are often at risk of lacking the power required to disentangle the independent contributions of multiple variables.
source: As a consequence, single studies are often at risk of lacking the power required to disentangle the independent contributions of multiple variables.
evidence: This is a general principle about statistical power applied to the specific context.

claim: Yarkoni et al., 2008 reported that activity in the visual word form area (VWFA) was significantly modulated by lexical frequency.
source: In a naturalistic rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) reading experiment, Yarkoni et al., 2008 reported an interesting incidental result: activity in the visual word form area (VWFA)—an area primarily associated with visual feature detection and orthography-phonology mapping (Dietz et al., 2005)—was significantly modulated by lexical frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The frequency effects in VWFA reported by Yarkoni et al., 2008 were robust to phonological and orthographic covariates.
source: Interestingly, these effects were robust to phonological and orthographic covariates, suggesting that VWFA activity may not only be involved in orthographic and phonological reading subprocesses, but also modulated by modality-independent lexical-semantic properties of linguistic input.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the cited study.

claim: Yarkoni et al., 2008 observed that frequency effects disappeared when controlling for lexical concreteness.
source: In addition, the authors observed that frequency effects disappeared when controlling for lexical concreteness.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the cited study.

claim: Yarkoni et al., 2008 speculated that the study may have lacked the power to disentangle the contributions of frequency and concreteness.
source: As the two variables were highly correlated, the authors speculated that the study may have lacked the power to disentangle their contributions and declared the results inconclusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the cited study.

claim: Neuroscout provides a wide range of linguistic annotations spanning phonological/orthographic word properties, semantic descriptors, and higher-level information-theoretic properties.
source: Neuroscout makes it possible to re-evaluate linguistic hypotheses in ecological stimuli using a wide range of linguistic annotations spanning both phonological/orthographic word properties (e.g. duration and phonological distinctiveness), semantic descriptors (e.g. valence, concreteness, sensorimotor attributes), and higher-level information-theoretic properties of language sequences (e.g. entropy in next-word prediction and word-by-word surprisal).
evidence: This is a description of the platform's linguistic features.

claim: The linguistic case study reimplemented analytic models from Yarkoni et al., 2008 across all Neuroscout datasets.
source: We reimplemented analytic models from Yarkoni et al., 2008 across all Neuroscout datasets, including regressors for word frequency, concreteness, speech, and control orthographic measures (number of syllables, number of phones, and duration), alongside a standard set of nuisance parameters.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: The resulting maps displayed significant VWFA effects for both frequency and concreteness.
source: The resulting maps displayed significant VWFA effects for both frequency and concreteness (Figure 6), corroborating the hypothesis of its involvement in lexical processing independent of presentation modality, and arguably in the context of language-to-imagery mapping.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Only 12 out of 33 tasks showed significant ROI-level association between VWFA and frequency at p<0.01.
source: Using a relatively liberal threshold of p<0.01, only 12 out of 33 tasks showed significant ROI-level association between VWFA and frequency, and only 5 tasks showed an association between VWFA and concreteness.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Only 5 out of 33 tasks showed significant ROI-level association between VWFA and concreteness at p<0.01.
source: Using a relatively liberal threshold of p<0.01, only 12 out of 33 tasks showed significant ROI-level association between VWFA and frequency, and only 5 tasks showed an association between VWFA and concreteness.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: In only one task was VWFA significantly associated with both frequency and concreteness.
source: In addition, in only one task was VWFA significantly associated with both frequency and concreteness.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: Meta-analysis overcomes power and stimulus variability limitations that can cause instability in dataset-level results.
source: By drawing on larger participant samples and more diverse stimuli, meta-analysis overcomes power and stimulus variability limitations that can cause instability in dataset-level results.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed results.

claim: Neuroscout seeks to promote the widespread adoption of reproducible and generalizable fMRI research practices.
source: Neuroscout seeks to promote the widespread adoption of reproducible and generalizable fMRI research practices, allowing users to easily test a wide range of hypotheses in dozens of open naturalistic datasets using automatically extracted neural predictors.
evidence: This is a statement of the platform's goals.

claim: Neuroscout is designed with a strong focus on reproducibility.
source: The platform is designed with a strong focus on reproducibility, providing a unified framework for fMRI analysis that reduces the burden of reproducible fMRI analysis and facilitates transparent dissemination of models and statistical results.
evidence: This is a description of the platform's design principles.

claim: Automatically extracted predictors can be used to test a wide range of hypotheses on naturalistic datasets without the need for costly manual annotation.
source: In particular, as we show in our meta-analyses, automatically extracted predictors can be used to test a wide range of hypotheses on naturalistic datasets without the need for costly manual annotation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the validation analyses.

claim: Neuroscout and pliers are designed to facilitate community-led expansion to novel extractors.
source: As a result, we have designed Neuroscout and its underlying feature extraction framework pliers to facilitate community-led expansion to novel extractors— made possible by the rapid increase in public repositories of pre-trained deep learning models such as HuggingFace (Abadi et al., 2015) and TensorFlow Hub (Abadi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the platform's extensibility design.

claim: Small participant samples and stimulus-specific effects can lead to misleading dataset-level results.
source: As we have pointed out in some of our examples, small participant samples and stimulus-specific effects can at times lead to misleading dataset-level results.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed results in the validation analyses.

claim: Automatically extracted predictors are particularly powerful when paired with Neuroscout's flexible model specification and execution workflow.
source: Automatically extracted predictors are particularly powerful when paired with Neuroscout's flexible model specification and execution workflow, as their combination makes it easy to operationalize hypotheses in identical ways across multiple diverse dataset and gather more generalizable consensus estimates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the demonstrated capabilities of the platform.

claim: Large-N studies are becoming increasingly common in cognitive neuroscience.
source: While large-N studies are becoming increasingly common in cognitive neuroscience, the importance of relying on large and diverse stimulus sets has been thus far underestimated (Westfall et al., 2016), placing Neuroscout in a unique position in the current research landscape.
evidence: This is presented as an observation about trends in the field, with citation supporting the claim about stimulus diversity.

claim: The importance of relying on large and diverse stimulus sets has been underestimated in cognitive neuroscience.
source: While large-N studies are becoming increasingly common in cognitive neuroscience, the importance of relying on large and diverse stimulus sets has been thus far underestimated (Westfall et al., 2016), placing Neuroscout in a unique position in the current research landscape.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: Neuroscout has paid close attention to ensuring transparency and reproducibility of statistical modeling by adopting a community-developed specification of statistical models.
source: We have paid close attention to ensuring transparency and reproducibility of statistical modeling by adopting a community-developed specification of statistical models, and developing accessible tools to specify, visualize and execute analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the platform's design approach.

claim: A major challenge in the analysis of naturalistic stimuli is the high degree of collinearity between features.
source: A major challenge in the analysis of naturalistic stimuli is the high degree of collinearity between features, as the interpretation of individual features is dependent on co-occurring features.
evidence: This is presented as a known challenge in naturalistic analysis.

claim: Controlling for confounding variables is critical for the interpretation of the primary feature in many cases.
source: In many cases, controlling for confounding variables is critical for the interpretation of the primary feature— as is evident in our investigation of the relationship between FFA and face perception.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the FFA case study.

claim: Neuroscout is designed to be agnostic to the goals of the user and empower them to construct sensibly designed models through comprehensive model reports.
source: Absent a consensus on how to model naturalistic data, we designed Neuroscout to be agnostic to the goals of the user and empower them to construct sensibly designed models through comprehensive model reports.
evidence: This is a description of the platform's design philosophy.

claim: An ongoing goal of the platform is to expand the visualizations and quality control reports to enable users to better understand the predictors and their relationship.
source: An ongoing goal of the platform—especially as the number of features continues to increase—will be to expand the visualizations and quality control reports to enable users to better understand the predictors and their relationship.
evidence: This is a statement about future development plans.

claim: A critical future direction for Neuroscout will be to implement statistical models which are optimized to estimate a large number of covarying targets.
source: However, as the number of features continues to grow, a critical future direction for Neuroscout will be to implement statistical models which are optimized to estimate a large number of covarying targets.
evidence: This is a statement about future development plans.

claim: Regularized encoding models, such as banded-ridge regression, have the advantage of implementing feature-space selection and variance partitioning methods.
source: Of note are regularized encoding models, such as the banded-ridge regression as implemented by the Himalaya package (Latour et al., 2022). These models have the additional advantage of implementing feature-space selection and variance partitioning methods, which can deal with the difficult problem of model selection in highly complex feature spaces such as naturalistic stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the Himalaya package.

claim: Neuroscout workflows are applicable to any BIDS-compliant dataset due to the flexibility of the BIDS Stats Model specification.
source: Although we have primarily focused on naturalistic datasets—as they intrinsically feature a high degree of reusability and ecological validity—Neuroscout workflows are applicable to any BIDS-compliant dataset due to the flexibility of the BIDS Stats Model specification.
evidence: This is a statement about the platform's capabilities.

claim: Indexing non-naturalistic fMRI datasets will be an important next step for Neuroscout.
source: Indexing non-naturalistic fMRI datasets will be an important next step, an effort that will be supported by the proliferation of data sharing portals and require the widespread sharing of harmonized preprocessed derivatives that can be automatically ingested.
evidence: This is a statement about future development plans.

claim: Dataset decay can occur from repeated sequential re-analysis.
source: In addition, as Neuroscout grows to facilitate the re-analysis of a broader set of public datasets, it will be important to reckon with the threat of 'dataset decay' which can occur from repeated sequential re-analysis (Thompson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: Neuroscout is designed to minimize undocumented researcher degrees of freedom by encouraging the central registration of all analysis attempts and associated results.
source: By encouraging the central registration of all analysis attempts and the associated results, Neuroscout is designed to minimize undocumented researcher degrees of freedom and link the final published results with all previous attempts.
evidence: This is a description of the platform's design to address dataset decay.

claim: Long-term maintenance, development, and user support is an on-going challenge for scientific software tools.
source: An on-going challenge for scientific software tools—especially those that rely on centralized services—is long-term maintenance, development, and user support.
evidence: This is presented as a known challenge in scientific software development.

claim: Government funding generally prefers novel research to the on-going maintenance of existing tools.
source: This problem is exacerbated for projects primarily supported by government funding, which generally prefers novel research to the on-going maintenance of existing tools.
evidence: This is presented as a known characteristic of funding mechanisms.

claim: Core components of Neuroscout are designed with modularity as a guiding principle to maximize longevity and impact.
source: With this in mind, we have designed many of the core components of Neuroscout with modularity as a guiding principle in order to maximize the longevity and impact of the platform.
evidence: This is a description of the platform's design philosophy.

claim: Components of Neuroscout are designed to be independently useful to encourage broader adoption by the community.
source: Although components of the platform are tightly integrated, they are also designed to be independently useful, increasing their general utility, and encouraging broader adoption by the community.
evidence: This is a description of the platform's design philosophy.

claim: The analyses presented in the paper are based on 13 naturalistic fMRI datasets sourced from various open data repositories.
source: The analyses presented in this paper are based on 13 naturalistic fMRI datasets sourced from various open data repositories (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the data used in the analyses.

claim: Several datasets spanned various original studies or distinct stimuli, resulting in 35 unique 'tasks' or 'studies' available for analysis.
source: Several datasets spanned various original studies or distinct simuli (e.g. Narratives, NNDb), resulting in 35 unique 'tasks' or 'studies' available for analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the data structure.

claim: Neuroscout datasets are uniformly preprocessed using FMRIPREP (version 1.2.2).
source: Neuroscout datasets are uniformly preprocessed using FMRIPREP (version 1.2.2) (Esteban et al., 2020; Esteban et al., 2019; Esteban et al., 2022), a robust NiPype-based MRI preprocessing pipeline.
evidence: This is a description of the preprocessing method, supported by citations.

claim: Visual features were extracted from video stimuli at a frequency of 1 Hz.
source: Visual features were extracted from video stimuli at a frequency of 1 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption.

claim: A well-validated cascaded convolutional network trained to detect the presence of faces was applied for face detection.
source: 'Faces': we applied a well-validated cascaded convolutional network trained to detect the presence of faces (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption with citation.

claim: Clarifai's General Image Recognition model was used to compute the probability of the presence of buildings in each frame.
source: 'Building': We used Clarifai's General Image Recognition model to compute the probability of the presence of buildings in each frame.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption.

claim: Spoken word frequency codes for the lexical frequency of words in the transcript, as determined by the SubtlexUS database.
source: 'Spoken word frequency' codes for the lexical frequency of words in the transcript, as determined by the SubtlexUS database (Brysbaert and New, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption with citation.

claim: Language features are extracted using speech transcripts with precise word-by-word timing determined through forced alignment.
source: Language features are extracted using speech transcripts with precise word-by-word timing determined through forced alignment.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption.

claim: Neuroscout leverages state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms to automatically extract hundreds of novel neural predictors from the original experimental stimuli.
source: Neuroscout leverages state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms to automatically extract hundreds of novel neural predictors from the original experimental stimuli.
evidence: This is a description of the platform's feature extraction capabilities.

claim: Feature values are ingested directly with no in place modifications, with the exception of down sampling of highly dense variables to 3 hz.
source: Feature values are ingested directly with no in place modifications, with the exception of down sampling of highly dense variables to 3 hz to facilitate storage on the server.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method.

claim: Brightness is computed as the average luminosity for pixels across the entire image.
source: We computed brightness (average luminosity) for frame samples of videos by computing the average luminosity for pixels across the entire image.
evidence: This is a description of the feature extraction method.

claim: Clarifai's 'General' model is a pre-trained deep convolutional neural network (CNN) for multi-class classification of over 11,000 categories of visual concepts.
source: We used Clarifai's 'General' model, a pre-trained deep convolutional neural network (CNN) for multi-class classification of over 11,000 categories of visual concepts, including objects and themes.
evidence: This is a description of the Clarifai model.

claim: Face detection, alignment, and cropping are performed through Multi-task Cascaded Convolutional Networks (MTCNN).
source: First, face detection, alignment, and cropping are performed through Multi-task Cascaded Convolutional Networks (MTCNN; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the face detection method, supported by citation.

claim: FaceNet is a face recognition deep CNN based on the Inception ResNet v1 architecture.
source: FaceNet is a face recognition deep CNN based on the Inception ResNet v1 architecture that achieved state-of-the-art performance when released (Schroff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the FaceNet model, supported by citation.

claim: The FaceNet recognition model used was pre-trained on the VGGFace2 dataset.
source: The particular recognition model we used was pre-trained on the VGGFace2 dataset (Cao et al., 2018), which is composed of over three million faces 'in the wild', encompassing a wide range of poses, emotions, lighting, and occlusion conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the model training, supported by citation.

claim: FaceNet creates a 512-dimensional embedding vector from cropped faces.
source: FaceNet creates a 512-dimensional embedding vector from cropped faces that represents extracted face features; thus more similar faces are closer in the euclidean embedding space.
evidence: This is a description of the FaceNet output.

claim: The Chinese Whispers clustering algorithm was used to group faces into coherent clusters.
source: We used the Chinese Whispers clustering algorithm, as this algorithm subjectively grouped faces into coherent clusters better than other commonly used algorithms (e.g. k-means clustering).
evidence: This is a description of the clustering method.

claim: Clustering resulted in 50–200 clusters that subjectively corresponded to readily identifiable characters across the video stimulus.
source: Depending on the dataset, this resulted in 50–200 clusters that subjectively corresponded to readily identifiable characters across the video stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the clustering results.

claim: Librosa was used to compute root-mean-squared (RMS) as a measure of instantaneous audio power over time.
source: We used librosa (McFee et al., 2015), a python package for music and audio analysis, to compute root-mean-squared (RMS) as a measure of the instantaneous audio power over time, or 'loudness'.
evidence: This is a description of the audio feature extraction method, supported by citation.

claim: The Forced Alignment and Vowel Extraction toolkit (FAVE) was used for force alignment of transcripts.
source: We force aligned the transcripts to extract word-level speech timing, using the Forced Alignment and Vowel Extraction toolkit (FAVE; Rosenfelder et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the forced alignment method, supported by citation.

claim: Rev.com provides human-created transcripts which are then force-aligned using proprietary methods.
source: Rev.com provides human-created transcripts which are then force-aligned using proprietary methods to produce a high-quality, aligned transcript, similar to that generated by the FAVE algorithm.
evidence: This is a description of the Rev.com service.

claim: Word frequency norms used in the analyses are from SUBTLEX-US, a 51 million words corpus of American English subtitles.
source: For all the analyses reported here, we used frequency norms from SUBTLEX-US (Brysbaert and New, 2009), a 51 million words corpus of American English subtitles.
evidence: This is a description of the lexical database used, supported by citation.

claim: Concreteness norms were extracted from the Brysbaert et al., 2014 concreteness database.
source: Concreteness norms were extracted from the (Brysbaert et al., 2014) concreteness database, which contains norms for over 40,000 English words, obtained from participants' ratings on a five-point scale.
evidence: This is a description of the lexical database used, supported by citation.

claim: The Massive Auditory Lexical Decision (MALD) database includes a variety of lexical, orthographic, and phonological descriptors for over 35,000 English words and pseudowords.
source: The Massive Auditory Lexical Decision (MALD) database (Tucker et al., 2019) is a large-scale auditory and production dataset that includes a variety of lexical, orthographic, and phonological descriptors for over 35,000 English words and pseudowords.
evidence: This is a description of the MALD database, supported by citation.

claim: Neuroscout uses FitLins for executing multi-level fMRI general linear model (GLM) analyses.
source: Neuroscout uses FitLins, a newly developed workflow for executing multi-level fMRI general linear model (GLM) analyses defined by the BIDS StatsModels specification.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis workflow.

claim: Model estimation at the first level was performed using AFNI.
source: Model estimation at the first level was performed using AFNI—in part due to its memory efficiency—and subject and group level summary statistics were fit using the nilearn.glm module.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: NiMARE (version 0.0.11rc1) was used to perform meta-analyses across the neuroscout datasets.
source: NiMARE (version 0.0.11rc1; available at: https://github.com/neurostuff/NiMARE; RRID:SCR_017398) was used to perform meta-analyses across the neuroscout datasets.
evidence: This is a description of the meta-analysis tool used.

claim: The DerSimonian & Laird random effects meta-regression algorithm was used for meta-analysis.
source: We used the DerSimonian & Laird random effects meta-regression algorithm (DerSimonian and Laird, 1986; Kosmidis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the meta-analysis method, supported by citations.
